sections.contenu_markdown: 'Since' has two lives in English: a marker of time, and a synonym of 'because' — context decides which one is meant.

items: Cause and effect relationships between two sentences

sections.contenu_markdown: 'Because' introduces the cause of an action described in the main clause. 'Since', when not used as a time marker, functions the same way, and can also start the sentence, followed by a comma before the main clause.

sections.enonce_markdown: Combine: 'Wome and Tanda took a motorcycle. There were no taxis.' (because)

etapes.justification: No taxis = cause; took a motorcycle = result.
Introduces the cause after the result.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Wome and Tanda took a motorcycle because there were no taxis.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The two sentences are linked into one causal sentence.

items.erreur_markdown: Confusing time-'since' (from a point in time) with reason-'since' (because).
items.pourquoi_faux: The two uses of 'since' are grammatically identical in form but semantically different; context (two simultaneous facts, not a duration) signals the reason meaning.
items.correction_markdown: Check whether the sentence describes a duration from a past point (time-since) or a cause-effect relationship (reason-since).

items.enonce_markdown: Combine using 'because': 'He stayed home. He was sick.'
items.solution_markdown: He stayed home because he was sick.

items_markdown: 'Because' introduces the cause of an action
'Since' can mean 'because' (reason) in addition to its time meaning
